title: {{NAME}} and the Last Wild Hero
moral: The world's wild places need as many defenders as its cities.
character_anchor: Bright children's book cartoon illustration, bold outlines, vivid flat colours. {{NAME}}, a young boy with brown hair and blue eyes, wearing a deep teal hero cape over a white suit with silver wing details, teal boots — same child, same face, same exact outfit in every image.

pages.content:
Most heroes protected cities.

{{NAME}} protected the coast, specifically the cliffs and coves north of the lighthouse, where sea birds nested and seals hauled out and the wild things happened that nobody organised and nobody reported.

His partner: a unicorn named Tide, whose horn glowed blue-green like sea glass and who could walk on water, which was practically a superpower in this job.

They had been at it two years. They had stopped four oil spills (small), relocated six abandoned seal pups, and convinced a wandering cargo ship captain that the rocks he was about to hit were real.

pages.content:
The crisis: a pod of dolphins had followed a warm current north and were now cut off from their return route by an unusual cold barrier.

Tide read the water temperatures with her horn: the cold barrier was two kilometres wide. Too wide for the dolphins to pass without serious risk.

"Options?" said {{NAME}}.

Tide showed him in images: a channel in the barrier that would open naturally in four days.

"We keep them comfortable for four days," said {{NAME}}. "And we call in the marine station for food support."

pages.content:
Four days of dolphin management.

Tide could communicate with them enough to keep them in the warm cove: a long, patient song from her horn that the dolphins responded to with a kind of reassured settling.

{{NAME}} handled logistics: the marine station's fish supply, keeping boats away from the area, monitoring the cold barrier.

On day three, a seal pup arrived and joined the dolphins, apparently also waiting something out.

"Wildlife does not tell you its plans," {{NAME}} noted in his report.

Tide made the particular rippling sound that was her version of agreement.

pages.content:
Day four: the barrier opened.

Tide read it first: a shift in the water's feel against her horn.

"Go," she said, in the way that unicorns say things.

She led the dolphins herself, walking into deeper water, her horn casting a clear blue-green line toward the open passage.

The dolphins followed. The seal pup followed the dolphins for one hundred metres, then peeled away toward its own destination.

{{NAME}} watched from the cliff until every fin had disappeared.

pages.content:
He sat on the cliff as the sea settled back into its normal patterns.

Four days. No coverage. No report in the news. The dolphins did not know what he and Tide had done and would not remember his face.

He thought: this is exactly what it's for.

Tide walked out of the water and shook herself and stood beside him.

They watched the horizon for a while.

He walked home along the cliff path as the sun went down, his cape damp with sea spray, absolutely satisfied.

In bed, he fell asleep to the sound of waves.
